prompt.context_jp: 深夜の本部フロアに人影はほとんどなく、相馬健のデスクだけ___蛍光灯の下で白く浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬健のデスクだけ___蛍光灯の下で白く浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits here? The sentence picks out Souma's desk as the ONE thing visible on an otherwise empty floor.

feedback.correct_en: 「だけが」marks exhaustive identification — of all possible things, Souma's desk is the only one lit up. New, scene-setting information takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「だけは」would imply contrast ('his desk, at least, was lit') suggesting other desks might also fit the description. 「を」is ungrammatical because 浮かんでいた is intransitive.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼のデスクだけが光っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Only his desk was lit (exhaustive listing).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼のデスクだけは光っていた。
contrast_examples.en: His desk, at least, was lit (contrastive implication).

prompt.context_jp: 夜が明けても、花咲舞___自分の部屋のデスクを離れなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 夜が明けても、花咲舞___自分の部屋のデスクを離れなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Mai is the established topic of this scene. Pick the particle.

feedback.correct_en: Mai has already been introduced; this sentence tells us WHAT she did (didn't leave her desk), so she's framed as the topic with は.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「が」would announce Mai as new information ('it was Mai who didn't leave'), which doesn't match — the camera is just following her.

contrast_examples.en: Mai (as for her) was home — topic.
It was Mai who was home — new info/identification.

prompt.context_jp: 窓の外では、いつもと変わらぬ朝の街___動き始めている。
prompt.prompt_jp: いつもと変わらぬ朝の街___動き始めている。
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator pans to a new scene outside the window. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: A fresh element appears in the narrative frame — the morning town is introduced as new, observed information, so が.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「は」would treat the morning town as an established topic being discussed, but here it's a sudden visual contrast to Mai's stalled night.

contrast_examples.en: Rain started falling (newly perceived).
Rain (as a topic) is cold (general statement).

prompt.context_jp: 上座に構えるの___、業務本部長の真藤毅である。
prompt.prompt_jp: 上座に構えるの___、業務本部長の真藤毅である。
prompt.prompt_en: A cleft-style sentence identifying who sits at the head seat. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: This is a presentational cleft: 「〜のは…である」(the one who X is Y). The topic-the-description, identify-the-person pattern uses は.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「のが」is possible in some embedded contexts, but as a standalone identifying sentence 「のは…である」is the natural, written-style frame.

contrast_examples.en: The one who came is Tanaka.
Tanaka came (new info).

prompt.context_jp: 川島の肩___わずかに強張ったのを、花咲は横目で確かめた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 川島の肩___わずかに強張ったのを、花咲は横目で確かめた。
prompt.prompt_en: This is the content Hanasaki observed. Which particle marks Kawashima's shoulder inside the embedded clause?

feedback.correct_en: Inside a subordinate 「〜のを」clause reporting a perception, the subject takes が. The main topic is 花咲, marked by は in the matrix clause.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「は」would try to make the shoulder a topic, but subordinate perception clauses almost never allow a topic は — the observed event is reported as a whole with が inside.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の手が震えるのを見た。
contrast_examples.en: I saw her hand tremble (embedded subject = が).
As for her, her hand trembled (matrix topic).

prompt.context_jp: 全員の視線が集まる中、姿を見せたの___相馬健だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 姿を見せたの___相馬健だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Everyone turns to look — then the sentence names who appeared. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: This is a cleft 「〜のは…だった」: the description ('the one who appeared') is set up as topic, and Souma is identified as the answer.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「のが…だった」would be ungrammatical in this slot. The 'answer-reveal' cleft pattern always uses のは…だ.

contrast_examples.jp: 助けてくれたのは彼だった。
contrast_examples.en: The one who helped me was him.
He helped me (plain subject = が).

prompt.context_jp: 大前さん___書いた推薦文の評価は なぜか最低でした。
prompt.prompt_jp: 大前さん___書いた推薦文の評価は なぜか最低でした。
prompt.prompt_en: Inside the relative clause '…が書いた推薦文' / '…は書いた推薦文'. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: In a relative clause modifying 推薦文, the embedded subject (the writer) takes が. The real topic of the whole sentence is 評価, marked outside by は.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「は」cannot occur inside this relative clause — は almost never marks a subject deep inside a modifier noun phrase.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が書いた本は面白い。
contrast_examples.en: The book he wrote is interesting.
He wrote a book (main-clause topic).

prompt.context_jp: 静かな時間を破ったの___、廊下を駆けてくる同期たちの足音だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 静かな時間を破ったの___、…足音だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Another cleft pattern — 'what broke the silence was…'. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: 「〜のは…だった」cleft frames the description as topic and reveals the answer in the predicate. That's a textbook は use.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「のが」with 〜だった at the end would be ungrammatical in this standalone identifying sentence.

contrast_examples.jp: 沈黙を破ったのはベルの音だった。
contrast_examples.en: What broke the silence was the bell.

contrast_examples.jp: ベルの音が沈黙を破った。
contrast_examples.en: The bell broke the silence (plain subject = が).

prompt.context_jp: 二人の間に落ちた沈黙___、決して気まずいものではなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 二人の間に落ちた沈黙___、決して気まずいものではなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator is pointedly denying one possible interpretation of the silence. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: The silence is presented as topic, with a contrastive flavor: 'this silence (unlike what you might expect) was not awkward.' Contrastive/topical は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce the silence as brand-new information, but the silence has already been established in the preceding scene.

contrast_examples.en: Today (in contrast to other days) is not cold.
Today is the cold day (identifying).

prompt.context_jp: 花咲の声___会議室に響き渡り、余韻だけが残った。
prompt.prompt_jp: 花咲の声___会議室に響き渡り、余韻だけが残った。
prompt.prompt_en: A dramatic beat describing an event. Which particle for 花咲の声?

feedback.correct_en: This is a single-event narration: the voice ringing out is new, scene-shifting information after Mai's outburst. Narrative が.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「花咲の声は」would turn the voice into a topic being discussed, which breaks the immediacy of the moment.

contrast_examples.en: The bell rang out (new event).
The sound of the bell is pleasant (general topic).

prompt.context_jp: 井脇は資料の束___丁寧に抱え、相馬のデスクにそっと積み上げた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 井脇は資料の束___丁寧に抱え、…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks what Iwaki is cradling?

feedback.correct_en: 抱える is a transitive verb — the thing being held is the direct object, marked by を.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「が」would make the stack the subject (impossible with 抱える), and 「に」would mark a location/goal.

contrast_examples.en: To hold a book (direct object).
The book falls (intransitive subject).

prompt.context_jp: 井脇悟は始発の電車___本部へ駆けつけていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 井脇悟は始発の電車___本部へ駆けつけていた。
prompt.prompt_en: How did he get there? Which particle marks the means?

feedback.correct_en: で marks the means of transportation: 電車で = 'by train'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「に」would mark a destination or arrival point (the train isn't where he's going), and 「を」would mark a path like 道を歩く.

contrast_examples.en: Go by bus (means).
Get on the bus (goal of 乗る).

prompt.context_jp: 花咲舞は川島奈津子の自宅___訪ねていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 花咲舞は川島奈津子の自宅___訪ねていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits with 訪ねる here?

feedback.correct_en: 訪ねる takes を for the place/person being visited — the destination is treated as a direct object.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「に」works with 行く/来る but with 訪ねる the standard pattern is 〜を訪ねる. 「で」would mark a location of action.

contrast_examples.en: To visit a friend (を).
To go to a friend's place (へ/に).

prompt.context_jp: 玄関先に立つ奈津子の顔___、記事が世に出た日から目に見えて痩せていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 玄関先に立つ奈津子の顔___、…目に見えて痩せていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking Natsuko's face as the subject of this descriptive sentence.

feedback.correct_en: A descriptive characterization ('her face had thinned since…') with Natsuko as the established figure in the scene — classic topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「が」would announce the face as new information, but we already know Natsuko is at the door; the narrator is now describing her state.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女の顔は青ざめていた。
contrast_examples.en: Her face had grown pale (descriptive topic).
(Her) face went pale (new event).

prompt.context_jp: 呼び出された川島奈津子___、部屋の空気に押し潰されそうな顔で戸口に立ち尽くしている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 呼び出された川島奈津子___、…戸口に立ち尽くしている。
prompt.prompt_en: Natsuko has just been summoned. The sentence then tells us how she looks. Which particle?

feedback.correct_en: Natsuko is the already-anchored character in this scene; the sentence describes her state, so topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would frame her as a brand-new participant, but she's been under discussion throughout the chapter.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は戸口に立っていた。
contrast_examples.en: He was standing in the doorway (topic).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が戸口に立っていた。
contrast_examples.en: He was the one standing in the doorway (identifying).

prompt.context_jp: 幾多の窮地を切り抜けてきた男の表情に___、微塵の揺らぎもない。
prompt.prompt_jp: …男の表情に___、微塵の揺らぎもない。
prompt.prompt_en: A negative existence pattern with a contrastive feel. Which particle attaches to に?

feedback.correct_en: 「には…ない」is the standard contrastive-negative frame: 'in his face, there isn't a trace of…'. The に+は combination highlights the location as topic/contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「には」is grammatical; 「にが」is not — が cannot stack onto に this way.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の目には涙がなかった。
contrast_examples.en: There were no tears in his eyes (contrastive location).
There are tears in (his) eyes (plain).

prompt.context_jp: 当行で働く3万人の行員たちの顔に ___ を塗ることになるんだぞ！
prompt.prompt_jp: 3万人の行員たちの顔に ___ を塗ることになるんだぞ！
prompt.prompt_en: What idiom is Omae using to threaten Natsuko? '…の顔に＿を塗る'

feedback.correct_en: 「顔に泥を塗る」is the fixed idiom for 'drag someone's name through the mud / disgrace them'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 墨 and 塩 are not part of this idiom. 「顔に泥を塗る」is the only standard form.

contrast_examples.en: Don't bring shame to your parents.
Rub salt in the wound (different idiom).

prompt.context_jp: お言葉を ___ ようですが…
prompt.prompt_jp: お言葉を ___ ようですが…
prompt.prompt_en: Souma's polite preface before contradicting Omae. Fill in the verb.

feedback.correct_en: 「お言葉を返すようですが」is a set polite phrase meaning 'I hate to contradict you, but…' — used to politely push back on a superior.
feedback.incorrect_en: 戻す and 送る don't form fixed humble phrases here; only 返す fits the idiom.

contrast_examples.jp: お言葉を返すようですが、違います。
contrast_examples.en: With respect, that's not correct.
To return a book (literal use of 返す).

prompt.context_jp: 他人の傷を ___ 起こす手伝いは、多くの行員にとって苦手な領域だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 他人の傷を ___ 起こす手伝いは…
prompt.prompt_en: What verb collocates with 傷 and 起こす to mean 'dig up (old wounds)'?

feedback.correct_en: 「掘り起こす」= dig up (something buried, including past wounds). It fits the metaphor of unearthing hidden painful history.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「引き起こす」means 'cause/trigger (an incident)', and 「持ち起こす」isn't a standard verb — neither captures 'dig up old wounds'.

contrast_examples.en: Dig up the past.
Cause an incident.

prompt.context_jp: 臨店の方が イチ行員のために こんなふうに ___ してくださるなんて
prompt.prompt_jp: イチ行員のために こんなふうに ___ してくださるなんて
prompt.prompt_en: Iwaki is thanking Souma for 'going to great lengths' for one employee. Fill in the noun.

feedback.correct_en: 「尽力する」= devote one's efforts (on behalf of someone). Fits the respectful register and the sense of going out of one's way for another person.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「努力」is general self-directed 'effort' (not toward someone else), and 「協力」means 'cooperate' which needs a partner, not a beneficiary.

contrast_examples.jp: 部下のために尽力する。
contrast_examples.en: Devote effort for one's subordinate.
Make an effort alone.

prompt.context_jp: 自分が他の人より偉いと思う人間だけが手にできる、冷ややかな ___ がその横顔にはあった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冷ややかな ___ がその横顔にはあった。
prompt.prompt_en: What is Shindo's calm, superior air described as?

feedback.correct_en: 「余裕」= composure, poise. 「冷ややかな余裕」paints his cold confidence as a bully who feels in control.
feedback.incorrect_en: 焦り (impatience) and 怒り (anger) contradict the whole description of him calmly looking at the ceiling without wavering.

contrast_examples.en: He had composure.
He showed impatience.

prompt.context_jp: 奈津子は壁に手を添え、崩れそうな膝を ___ 支えている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 崩れそうな膝を ___ 支えている。
prompt.prompt_en: Natsuko is barely holding herself up after the ordeal. Pick the adverb.

feedback.correct_en: 「どうにか支える」= 'somehow managing to support' — matches her fragile, barely-standing state.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「さっさと」(briskly) and 「うっかり」(carelessly) contradict the image of someone fighting not to collapse.

contrast_examples.en: I was somehow still standing.

contrast_examples.jp: さっさと立ち上がった。
contrast_examples.en: He stood up quickly.

prompt.context_jp: 大前が本部長に取り入って便宜を図ってもらおうとする、その筋書きを ___ には十分な材料であった。
prompt.prompt_jp: その筋書きを ___ には十分な材料であった。
prompt.prompt_en: Souma's documents are enough to do what to Omae's scheme?

feedback.correct_en: 「筋書きを崩す」= to break down / dismantle (someone's) scenario. It's the standard collocation for undoing a planned narrative.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「壊す」is used for physical destruction; 「折る」is for breaking/snapping physical things. Neither pairs idiomatically with 筋書き.

contrast_examples.en: Dismantle a plan.
Break a toy (physical).

prompt.context_jp: 何かしてあげたいという思いだけが ___ して、舞は掛ける言葉を選びかねた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 何かしてあげたいという思いだけが ___ して…
prompt.prompt_en: Mai's wish to help goes nowhere. Which verb captures 'spinning in place / idling fruitlessly'?

feedback.correct_en: 「空回りする」= to spin uselessly, go nowhere — a perfect metaphor for intentions that produce no action.
feedback.incorrect_en: 「回転」is neutral 'rotation', 「周回」is 'circling/orbiting'. Neither carries the futile-effort nuance.

contrast_examples.en: One's feelings go nowhere.
A tire rotates (neutral).

prompt.context_jp: Souma politely challenges Omae in the executive meeting.
prompt.prompt_en: Which opening sounds more natural when a subordinate carefully pushes back on a superior in a formal meeting?

choices.text: お言葉を返すようですが、川島さんとの間に、何らかのトラブルがあったからではないんですか？
でも違うと思うんだけど、川島さんとなんかトラブルがあったからじゃない？

feedback.correct_en: In a boardroom confronting a superior, the formulaic 「お言葉を返すようですが」softens direct contradiction and sustains humble register. Option B is casual peer speech that would be shockingly rude here.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B lacks keigo and uses casual connectors (〜じゃない、なんか) that would be unthinkable in front of 本部長.

contrast_examples.jp: お言葉を返すようですが、違うと思います。
contrast_examples.en: With respect, I think you're mistaken (business polite).

contrast_examples.jp: でも違うと思うんだけど。
contrast_examples.en: But I think you're wrong (casual, peer).

prompt.context_jp: Natsuko thanks Mai after the meeting — close-friend conversation.
prompt.prompt_en: Which reply from Mai sounds most natural to a close friend thanking you?

choices.text: いいえ、どういたしまして。
とんでもございません。

feedback.correct_en: Between best friends, Mai's warm 「ううん」('nah, it's nothing') is the natural intimate response. The scene is a quiet, personal moment.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is politely neutral — fine with acquaintances but overly formal between close friends. C is business-level humble language, completely out of place.

contrast_examples.jp: ありがとう。／ううん、気にしないで。
contrast_examples.en: Thanks. / No, don't worry (close friends).

contrast_examples.jp: ありがとうございます。／とんでもございません。
contrast_examples.en: Thank you. / Not at all (customer/business).

prompt.context_jp: Shindo pressures Natsuko to retract her accusation, pretending to offer the 'best way forward'.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing matches an executive's polished pressure tactic — superficially polite but closing the exit?

choices.text: 私の提案が、東京第一銀行がこれ以上傷つかない最善の方法だと思うが…違うかね？
俺の提案で銀行がこれ以上傷つかないのが一番いいじゃん、違う？

feedback.correct_en: A matches the actual story — written-style formal vocabulary (最善の方法, 違うかね) with a superior's commanding 〜かね tag. It projects authority without raising voice.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses 俺 and casual sentence endings (〜じゃん、違う？) that an executive would never use in a disciplinary meeting.

contrast_examples.jp: 最善の方法だと思うが、違うかね？
contrast_examples.en: I believe this is the best way — don't you agree? (executive register)
It's the best, right? (casual)

prompt.context_jp: Mai's emotional outburst at Omae — she declares she will never forgive him.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version delivers Mai's righteous anger most naturally in Japanese?

choices.text: 彼女の人生を狂わせたあなたを…私は絶対に許しません！
あなたは彼女の人生を狂わせたので、私は絶対に許さないと思います。

feedback.correct_en: A front-loads the accusation ('you who ruined her life…') and ends with the forceful declaration 「絶対に許しません」— natural for a climactic outburst.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is grammatically fine but reads like a calm written explanation. 「〜ので」+「〜と思います」drains all emotional punch from the moment.

contrast_examples.jp: あなたを絶対に許しません！
contrast_examples.en: I will absolutely never forgive you! (emotional)

contrast_examples.jp: あなたを許さないと思います。
contrast_examples.en: I don't think I'll forgive you (hedged, flat).

prompt.context_jp: Mai teases Souma at her family's diner.
prompt.prompt_en: Which exchange sounds like natural, informal teasing between Mai and her boss in a cozy family-diner setting?

choices.text: ま～た来たんですか、相馬さん。／悪いか？
またいらっしゃったのですね、相馬様。／はい、申し訳ありません。

feedback.correct_en: A's drawn-out 「ま～た」+「悪いか？」perfectly captures the half-joking banter the two share off-the-clock. The relationship allows this teasing register.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses customer-service keigo (いらっしゃる、〜様、申し訳ありません). Mai never addresses Souma like a hotel guest, and the scene would feel stiff.

contrast_examples.en: Here again? / Got a problem with that? (close banter)

contrast_examples.jp: またお越しくださいましたか？
contrast_examples.en: You've come again? (hotel-level keigo)
